title: The Christine Raid Incident
summary: Psyche raids Christine's stream bearing viewers as gifts. Christine responds with the banhammer. A point-by-point rebuttal of 'slanderous allegations' follows, delivered with the gravity of a UN tribunal and the energy of a wacky playhouse.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: closed, unresolved, eternally re-litigated.

The sequence of events, as preserved in the record: Psyche arrives at Christine's stream in the traditional manner of the raid — bringing viewers, goodwill, and chaos in roughly equal measure. The raid ends the way several diplomatic missions in cult history have ended: with a ban.

What followed was the now-canonical 'Point by Point Analysis of the Slanderous Allegations' — a full-episode rebuttal addressing each accusation in circulation, delivered point by point, with exhibits. Allegations were denied. Frustrations were aired. The phrase 'Christine's Wacky Playhouse' entered the permanent lexicon.

The Codex takes no position on who was right. The Codex notes only that the banhammer (see: The Banhammer, artifacts wing) claimed another entry in its ledger, and that the drama produced more content than the original raid ever could have.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: Full Poltergeist.
RECURRENCE RISK: guaranteed.

title: The Sweetie Impersonation Affair
summary: Panelist Arthur impersonates streamer 'Sweetie' convincingly enough to fool Christine and others. The panel becomes a masquerade. Trust in voices is never fully restored.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: declassified with mild embarrassment for all parties.

During a panel preserved in the archive, Arthur executed what the record describes as a successful impersonation of another streamer known as 'Sweetie' — successful enough that Christine and others engaged with the impostor as the genuine article.

The Codex wishes to stress the structural implications: if one panelist can be two people, the panel's true headcount is unknowable. Cult scholars refer to this as the Authentic-vs-Imposter Problem (see also: the authentic vs imposter Nick, characters wing), and it remains unsolved.

No lasting harm was recorded. Lasting suspicion, however, was archived in full.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: Elevated Nonsense.
LESSON, IF ANY: verify the voice before you confess to it.

title: The IP2 Infiltration Night
summary: Trolls from an outside faction flood the chat with threats while panelist conflicts flare simultaneously. The next stream is titled GOOD VIBES ONLY, which is how you know it was bad.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: sealed under the Good Vibes Accord.

The record describes a difficult night: chat infiltrated by an outside troll faction (identified on-stream as IP2) making threats of the ugliest varieties, while interpersonal conflicts among panelists flared on a second front. A two-theater war, fought live.

The response, preserved in the following broadcast, was doctrinally significant: a stream titled 'GOOD VIBES ONLY Open Panel, Browsing the Codex' — opening with an intense song about manipulation and false righteousness, followed by a relaxed, cat-filled panel. The cats, as ever, were the de-escalation mechanism (see: cats as content drivers, concepts wing).

The Codex classifies this as the canonical demonstration of the archive's oldest survival law: when the outside gets loud, browse the Codex and pet the cat.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: Full Poltergeist, downgraded to Mild Disturbance by feline intervention.

title: The Cash App Tribunal
summary: A malfunctioning text-to-speech opens the proceedings by reading an unrelated police roleplay. The community then conducts heated hearings on Cash App fraud claims, boundary violations, and alleged conspiracies. The TTS remains the most coherent speaker.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: ongoing; the tribunal never formally adjourned.

The session opened, per the record, with the text-to-speech system malfunctioning and reciting an unrelated police roleplay scenario to a bewildered court. The host attempted repairs. The machine had said what it came to say.

Proceedings then moved to the main docket: heated community commentary regarding Cash App fraud investigations, boundary violations, fake friendships, and allegations of conspiracy — with speaker Brown Bird entering extended testimony of frustration into the record.

The Codex notes for posterity that no verdict was reached, no funds were located, and the broken TTS delivered the evening's only uncontested statement.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: Elevated Nonsense with financial subplot.
EXHIBIT A: the machine that spoke out of turn.

title: The Whisper Network Wars
summary: A multi-episode campaign against the whisper networks — rumors, half-truths, and 600-pound trolls — fought with spoken-word poetry, strategic silence, and the occasional point-by-point airstrike.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: open. This war does not end; it merely changes channels.

Across a run of episodes in the archive ('I See the Board', 'My 600 Pound Troll', 'I'd Rather Just Hang Out Alone', 'The Stupidity is Painful'), the record documents a sustained campaign against what the host termed whisper networks: informal channels where half-truths circulate without accountability, letting crowds draw their own wrong conclusions on schedule.

The counter-arsenal, as deployed on-stream: theatrical spoken-word openings, strategic visibility, composure as a weapon, and the occasional full-episode rebuttal when composure had done all it could.

The Codex observes that every era of the cult has its whisper war, and every whisper war produces the era's best poetry. This is either alchemy or attrition. The scholars are divided, quietly, in a network of whispers.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: chronic, weaponized into art.

title: On Whisper Networks: A Field Guide to Rumors in Small Communities
summary: What the 'I See the Board' era taught the archive about how gossip actually works: half-truths over lies, implication over accusation, and why strategic visibility beats denial.
fullEntry:
Every small community eventually discovers it has a second communication system running underneath the first. The show's 'I See the Board' era put that system on the examination table.

The mechanics, as laid out on-stream, are worth preserving: whisper networks rarely traffic in outright lies. Lies are falsifiable. The efficient rumor is a half-truth — accurate enough to survive a fact-check, incomplete enough to mislead — passed along with a raised eyebrow rather than a claim. The crowd draws its own conclusions, and no individual node of the network ever said the false thing out loud. Accountability evaporates by design.

The counter-strategy documented in the archive is equally specific. Not denial — denial feeds the network, because a denial restates the rumor with your name attached. Instead: strategic visibility. Say what you are doing, in public, on the record, repeatedly, so the half-truth has to compete with a whole one. Composure as counterweapon; the record as rebuttal.

Whether it worked is a question the Drama Files can argue about (see: The Whisper Network Wars). But as a field theory of small-community gossip, it holds up better than most academic treatments — and it rhymed.

Filed under: things the show understood before it understood itself.

title: The Raid as Ritual: On Sending Your Audience Somewhere Else
summary: From kiss-for-100-viewers incentives to diplomatic incidents: what the archive's raid history says about the strangest gift economy in live streaming.
fullEntry:
The raid is the strangest ritual live streaming ever invented: at the end of a broadcast, a host takes their most valuable possession — a live audience — and gives it away to someone else, all at once, as a gift that arrives like a flood.

The archive documents the full spectrum of the form. At one end, the incentive raid: the recorded plan to raid Danny Stranger's stream with a kiss promised at the 100-viewer mark — the audience as dowry, the milestone as vow. At the other end, the diplomatic incident: the Christine raid, which ended in a ban and a full-episode point-by-point response (see: The Christine Raid Incident, Drama Files).

Between those poles sits the truth of the ritual. A raid is a gift that cannot be refused quietly. It says: here is everything I gathered tonight — deal with it. Received well, it builds alliances that outlast platforms. Received badly, it produces the finest drama in the record.

Either outcome feeds the archive, which may be why the show never stopped doing it. The Codex, which eats drama and goodwill with equal appetite, declines to recommend a policy.

Filed under: gift economies, occupational hazards of generosity.

title: The Ghost Confession
summary: A live, unscheduled confession of love — addressed to Ghost — detonates mid-broadcast. Chaos ensues, per the official title. The Codex classifies romance as a category of incident.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: open; matters of the heart do not close.

The record preserves an episode titled, in full: 'Live confession: I'm in love with you, Ghost — chaos ensues.' The archive's own summary confirms the essentials: a spontaneous declaration of love, delivered live, to a party identified as Ghost, followed by consequences the broadcast itself filed under chaos.

The Codex wishes to note the structural problem: a confession made on-stream is a confession made to everyone. The chat was present. The chat had opinions. The chat always has opinions.

Whether the sentiment was returned is not preserved in the summary, which the Codex considers the record's single greatest act of discretion.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: Full Poltergeist, romantic subtype.
FILED UNDER: love as cosmic violation (see concepts wing).

title: The Trixs Allegations Hearing
summary: Outside communities level claims about the welfare of Trixs the cat. The defense presents its evidence live: one visibly content cat, affectionate on camera, unbothered by proceedings.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: dismissed with prejudice by the cat.

During the episode preserved as 'Im the bad guy. these people are freaking insane,' the record shows Psyche responding to criticism and accusations from online communities — among them claims regarding the treatment of his cat, Trixs.

The defense strategy, as documented: present the animal. Trixs appeared on camera, demonstrated affection, and was argued — persuasively, per the record — to be happy and cared for.

The Codex notes that this is the second entry in the archive's long jurisprudence of feline exculpation (see: The Cat Defense, events wing; the Cat Question, basement). The cat has never lost a case. The cat does not know there are cases.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: Elevated Nonsense, resolved by purring.
EXHIBIT A: the cat, visibly fine.

title: The Gotti Disturbance
summary: Mid-broadcast, something smells off. A theatrical monologue on manipulation gives way to genuine unease, and a party identified only as Gotti enters the permanent record via the episode title.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: unresolved; the smell was never formally identified.

The episode opens, per the record, with an extended theatrical monologue about recognizing manipulation, gossip, and performative drama — strategic visibility, composure, the refusal to play along. Standard doctrine, delivered in high style.

Then the tone shifts. Something, in Psyche's assessment, felt off about the earlier broadcast activities. The episode title assigns responsibility with admirable economy: 'Something Smells Off..... Dammit Gotti.'

The Codex has no further information on Gotti, the nature of the smell, or the connection between them, and considers the five ellipsis points in the official title to be doing an extraordinary amount of evidentiary work.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: Mild Disturbance, olfactory-adjacent.
OUTSTANDING QUESTION: dammit, Gotti — what?

title: The StreamYard Vertical Crisis
summary: An episode titled simply WOW: community conflicts, payment app issues, and the true antagonist — StreamYard's vertical layout feature — litigated in a single rambling session.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: ongoing, like all platform grievances.

The episode preserved under the title 'WOW' is, per the record, a rambling and informal session touching community conflicts, moderation war stories, payment app trouble, and extended personal tangents. But the Codex identifies the true antagonist of the proceedings: StreamYard's vertical layout feature.

Every era of the cult has fought a war against its own tools (see: technical glitching as metaphor; Mars retrograde technical interference, concepts wing). The machines host the ritual, and the machines have opinions about aspect ratios.

The Codex notes that the episode title constitutes the entire official statement on these events, and endorses it as complete.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: Elevated Nonsense, 9:16.
LESSON: the layout is never just the layout.

title: The Shadowban Scare
summary: After an opening poem of mirrors, keys, and honey, Psyche addresses the possibility that the platform has quietly turned its face away: a potential shadowban, the most occult of all moderation actions.
fullEntry:
FILE STATUS: unfalsifiable, which is the whole problem.

The episode 'Let's Have a Beautiful Day!' opens with an extended spoken-word performance — identity, awakening, thresholds, mirrors, keys, honey, transformation — before descending to the material plane, where Psyche addresses the suspicion that he had been shadowbanned.

The Codex observes that the shadowban is the most genuinely occult mechanism in the entire streaming cosmology: an invisible judgment, delivered by a hidden authority, whose existence can be suspected but never confirmed, whose effects are measurable only as absence. No hex in the archive operates with such elegance.

Whether the ban was real is unrecorded. The beautiful day proceeded regardless, which the record presents as the actual doctrine.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: Mild Disturbance, metaphysically load-bearing.
FILED UNDER: judgments, invisible; days, beautiful anyway.
